reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: A rare chronic inflammatory disorder affecting one cerebral hemisphere, presenting most often in children with drug-resistant focal seizures
Epilepsia partialis continua, in which continuous focal motor seizure activity affects part of the body, is a characteristic feature
The clinical course brings progressive hemiparesis, cognitive decline and, when the dominant hemisphere is involved, language impairment
Serial MRI shows progressive unilateral hemispheric atrophy, often with insular and periventricular involvement
The presumed mechanism is a cell-mediated immune process with T-lymphocyte-driven inflammation and neuronal loss confined to one hemisphere
Immunotherapy may slow progression and help seizures, but definitive seizure control usually requires functional disconnection or hemispherectomy
Hemispherectomy typically stops the intractable seizures at the cost of a predictable fixed hemiparesis and visual field deficit
reference.pathophysiology: Rasmussen encephalitis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory disorder characteristically restricted to a single cerebral hemisphere. Histopathology shows T-cell-dominant perivascular inflammation, microglial nodules, reactive gliosis and progressive neuronal loss, supporting a predominantly cell-mediated cytotoxic process, although humoral and antigen-driven mechanisms have also been proposed. Ongoing inflammation drives relentless cortical damage and hemispheric atrophy, producing the combination of drug-resistant focal seizures, epilepsia partialis continua and progressive contralateral neurological and cognitive deficits.
additionalDifferentials: Focal cortical dysplasia and other structural epilepsies
Mitochondrial disease (e.g. MELAS) causing epilepsia partialis continua
additionalInvestigations: Serial brain MRI to demonstrate progressive unilateral hemispheric atrophy
Electroencephalography, including prolonged monitoring, showing unihemispheric slowing and epileptiform activity
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis including oligoclonal bands to support inflammation and exclude infection
Brain biopsy in selected cases to confirm characteristic inflammatory histopathology
PET or SPECT to assess unilateral hemispheric dysfunction
Autoimmune and metabolic screens to exclude mimics
redFlags: Epilepsia partialis continua that is refractory to antiseizure medication
Rapidly progressive hemiparesis or cognitive and language decline
Progressive hemispheric atrophy on serial imaging
reference.prognosis: Untreated, Rasmussen encephalitis progresses to a fixed severe hemiparesis, cognitive impairment and intractable seizures. Immunotherapy may modify the tempo, but seizure freedom generally requires hemispherectomy or hemispheric disconnection, which halts the epilepsy while leaving a predictable permanent motor and visual deficit; earlier surgery may better preserve overall function.
pitfalls: Attributing early focal seizures to ordinary focal epilepsy and missing the progressive inflammatory course
Delaying surgical referral in a dominant-hemisphere case for fear of deficits, allowing further decline
Failing to obtain serial imaging to demonstrate characteristic progressive atrophy
Overlooking mimics such as mitochondrial disease or a structural lesion before committing to diagnosis
